title: The wire that comes back late

data.source: Traced monoidal categories (Joyal, Street and Verity 1996) and categories with feedback (Katis, Sabadini and Walters 1997). Checked on random matrices and on one seeded noisy path of 60,000 steps.

prediction: Occasion, cut, seed is a process with feedback through a delay: a machine with a state. It is not a trace. Joined with no delay the seed would do nothing at all. The count C adds up when occasions are joined anywhere; the number of cuts adds up only when they are joined at a cut.
baseline: The laws of a trace (Joyal, Street and Verity 1996) and of delayed feedback (Katis, Sabadini and Walters 1997). Decoy: a box with no feedback wire.
why: All five predictions held. Shared: the loop is an arrow in a known kind of category, with the seed as its state (R5 is an ASSUMPTION in Phoenix; Phoenix lists "process grammar" among the candidates for what CRR is). Left over on the category side: laws of composition CRR does not use. Left over on the CRR side: the ruler and the half-turn, which the diagram does not see.

forks.box outputs the seed before the update: the instant trace is again the identity; not reported

result: The instant trace obeyed its laws on random matrices. The instant trace of the seed box came out as 1.0: with no delay the seed is a plain wire. With the delay, the pulled-straight loop returned every input exactly one step late (mean squared miss 2.009 of the variance), and under a steady input the seed fell short of the instant value by 0.7 after one occasion, 0.16807 after five and almost nothing after twenty: exactly q to the n. Sliding held with the seed carried along and failed by 0.432 without. On a path with 195 cuts, the count C added up in all 2000 random splits; the number of cuts failed to add up in 443 of them and in 0 of the 194 splits made at a cut.

framework.name: Process theories and traced monoidal categories
